questions.question: A girl and a boy stand still on smooth ice in their skates, a few metres apart, each holding one end of a rope. She gives the rope a hard tug, while he just holds on to his end. What happens to the two of them?
questions.answer: Both of them slide toward each other
choices: Both of them slide toward each other
Only he slides, since he is not pulling
Only she slides, pulling herself to him
Neither slides, since the two pulls balance
questions.context: As she tugs, the rope pulls her toward the boy, and he pulls back on his end just by holding on, so the rope pulls him toward her as well. Whatever is pulled pulls back, so both of them slide, and these two pulls do not cancel out. She would slide alone only if his end were tied to a post.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.7C has 6th graders identify the force pairs between interacting objects, and two skaters pulled together by one of them is the standard demonstration that the one who does nothing still pulls back.

questions.question: A swimmer sweeps her arms backward through the water, stroke after stroke, and glides forward across the pool. What pushes her forward?
questions.answer: The water, pushing on her hands
choices: The water, pushing on her hands
The water, closing in behind her body
The force she stores up with each stroke
Her arms, pulling on the rest of her body
questions.context: Her hands push the water backward, and the water pushes back on her hands, forward; that push from the water is what moves her along. Her arms cannot move her by pulling on her own body: they move her only by pushing on the water. She stores up no force either, since a force lasts only while two things act on each other.
questions.grade_note: A swimmer pushing water back and moving forward is a named example in the 6th-grade third-law line (curriculum map G6.P7, TEKS 6.7C).

questions.question: A spacecraft drifts far out in space, where there is no air at all. It fires its rocket engine, and hot gas blasts out of the back. What happens to the spacecraft?
questions.answer: It speeds up, pushed forward by the gas
choices: It speeds up, pushed forward by the gas
It stays put, with no air to push against
It speeds up, but less than it would in air
It drifts backward, along with the gas
questions.context: The engine pushes the gas out backward, and the gas pushes the rocket forward. A rocket never needs air to push against, and it works even better in empty space, where its exhaust escapes freely. A New York Times editorial mocked the rocket pioneer Robert Goddard on this point in 1920, and the paper printed a correction in July 1969, during the flight of Apollo 11.
questions.grade_note: A rocket's exhaust is a named 6th-grade third-law example (curriculum map G6.P7), and textbooks name the belief that a rocket pushes on the air as a common misconception.

questions.question: A bug flying over a highway smacks into the windshield of a speeding truck. The bug is squashed flat, while the truck rolls on as if nothing had happened. How hard does the bug push on the truck?
questions.answer: Just as hard as the truck pushes on it
choices: Just as hard as the truck pushes on it
Far more weakly than the truck pushes on it
A bit more weakly than the truck pushes on it
Not at all, since the bug is far too light
questions.context: Forces come in equal pairs, so in the crash the bug pushes on the truck exactly as hard as the truck pushes on the bug. The same-sized push changes the tiny, light bug's motion enormously and the heavy truck's hardly at all, which is why only the bug is squashed.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.7C teaches that a force pair is equal in size, and NGSS MS-PS2-1 applies the law to collisions, where students commonly believe the heavier object pushes harder.

questions.question: A batter swings, and the bat smacks a pitched baseball and sends it flying. The bat pushes on the ball, and the ball pushes back on the bat. Why do these two forces not cancel each other out?
questions.answer: Each one acts on a different object
choices: Each one acts on a different object
The bat pushes harder than the ball does
The ball pushes back a moment later
Forces pointing opposite ways never cancel
questions.context: The two pushes are equal, opposite and come at the same moment, but one acts on the ball and the other on the bat. Forces cancel only when they act on the same object, as two equal pulls on one rope do, so the bat's push sends the ball flying while the ball's push acts on the bat instead.
questions.grade_note: The 6th-grade third-law line (curriculum map G6.P7) ends on exactly this: the two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel.

questions.question: Isaac Newton's third law says that forces always come in pairs. A carpenter's hammer strikes a nail and drives it down into a board. Which force is the partner of the hammer's push on the nail?
questions.answer: The nail's push up on the hammer
choices: The nail's push up on the hammer
The board's push up on the nail
The hand's push down on the hammer
Earth's pull down on the nail
questions.context: A force pair is always the same two objects acting on each other: the hammer pushes on the nail, so the nail pushes back on the hammer, equally hard and the opposite way. The board's push is another force on the nail itself, so it belongs to a different pair, between the nail and the board.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.7C asks 6th graders to identify the force pairs that come from interactions between objects.

questions.question: An apple drops from a branch, pulled down by Earth's gravity. The apple pulls on Earth too. Why does no one ever see Earth move up to meet a falling apple?
questions.answer: Earth is so massive it barely moves
choices: Earth is so massive it barely moves
The apple's pull on Earth is far weaker
The two pulls cancel each other out
Earth's spin holds it firmly in place
questions.context: The apple pulls Earth up exactly as hard as Earth pulls the apple down, but Earth's mass is vastly larger, so the same-sized pull moves Earth far too little to notice while the apple drops to the ground. The two pulls act on different objects, so they cannot cancel, and Earth's spin has nothing to do with it.
questions.grade_note: NGSS PS2.A states the third law for any pair of interacting objects, gravity included, and 5th grade has already taught that more mass means less change in motion (Florida SC.5.P.13.3).

questions.question: A girl presses her hands against a heavy wooden door and pushes until it slowly swings open. Her hands push on the door, and the door pushes back on her hands. When does the door's push on her hands begin?
questions.answer: The moment she starts to push on it
choices: The moment she starts to push on it
Just after her push, in answer to it
Once the door starts to swing open
Once she pushes as hard as she can
questions.context: The two pushes of a pair always begin and end together. The instant she presses on the door, it presses back on her hands, before it has moved at all and however gently she starts. The name 'reaction' makes the door's push sound like an answer that comes second, but neither push comes first.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.7C asks 6th graders to identify simultaneous force pairs, and the curriculum line G6.P7 says the push back comes at the same moment.

2461650416.why: Judge (medium, tell): every child knows a skater who shoves a wall rolls back, the two 'stays put' choices were twins and 'rolls forward' was dead; the lead and judge (low) also found that 'a wall cannot push' repeats forces-and-net-force's brick ('stone cannot push') and T1's crate. Kept on the same fact, that the thing acted on acts back even when it does nothing, now as two skaters pulled together by a rope that only one of them pulls (UCSB demo 12.57, F21). Four live outcomes, each a recorded idea: only the passive one moves (M3), she pulls herself to him, the pulls balance (M1 by way of the T1 tug-of-war, M10). No sizes given (the mass effect is the apple's). The context avoids 'just as hard', 'at the same moment' and 'different objects', which other questions key.

43801836f9.why: Judge (medium, tell): 'The air above, pressing on her back' was a dead choice. Replaced, as the judge proposed, by the belief that a body moves itself with its own muscles ('Her arms, pulling on the rest of her body'; forces between the parts of one body cancel, F23). The key lost its word 'forward', which echoed the stem. The context no longer says 'just as hard' (the bug's key).

bb13d18c67.why: Judge (medium, tell): only one wrong choice was live. 'It slows down, held back by the gas' is replaced, as the judge proposed, by the other half of the push-on-the-air mistake, 'It speeds up, but less than it would in air' (false: rockets work better in a vacuum, F9). Stem and key unchanged; the context drops 'just as hard' (the bug's key).

added.6c052ec1b2: Replaces the dropped balloon (78962112bf) on the scope's 'at the same moment', which no question keyed (F2, F22). The wrong choices are the recorded mistake that the reaction comes after the action (M8: Wikipedia, 'even happening some time after the first'), the push back waiting for motion, and the push back waiting for a strong push. A still door, not a rolling skater, so the stem does not show the rope question's answer.

dropped.question: A girl blows up a balloon and pinches its neck shut, with the open end pointing at the floor. She lets go, and air streams out of the neck toward the floor. What does the balloon do, and why?
dropped.why: The lead and the judge (low): gas pushed out of a vessel pushes the vessel the other way is the rocket's mechanism, so the balloon repeated bb13d18c67; and the judge (medium) found that what a released balloon does is everyday experience, with two dead choices. Replaced by a question on the one core fact of the scope that no question keyed: the two forces of a pair begin at the same moment (TEKS 6.7C 'simultaneous').
